mcqs.question: A routing table has entries for both 172.16.0.0/16 and 172.16.5.0/24. A packet is destined for 172.16.5.10. Which entry does the router use?
options: 172.16.0.0/16, because broader entries are always checked first
Both entries equally, splitting the traffic between them
172.16.5.0/24, because it's the longest (most specific) matching prefix, which always wins over a broader match
Neither — an exact host-address entry would be required to match
mcqs.explanation: Longest prefix match always prefers the most specific matching entry, so the /24 wins over the broader /16 even though both technically match. There's no rule preferring broader entries first (the broader-entries-first claim), routers don't split single-packet traffic across matching entries (the traffic-splitting claim), and an exact host entry isn't required — the /24 network match is sufficient (the exact-host-entry-required claim is false).

mcqs.question: Why is a default route (0.0.0.0/0) always the last route considered, never the first, when a router has other matching entries available?
options: Because default routes have the lowest priority flag set by convention
Because ISPs configure default routes to activate only after a timeout period
Because default routes are only used when the router's static routes are disabled
Because 0.0.0.0/0 has the shortest possible prefix length, so by longest-prefix-match rules, any more specific entry will always be preferred over it
mcqs.explanation: The default route's 0-length prefix is, by definition, the least specific possible match, so longest-prefix-match logic naturally defers to it last — this isn't a separate priority flag, it falls directly out of the prefix-matching rule itself. There's no priority flag mechanism (the priority-flag claim), no dependency on static routes being disabled (the static-routes-disabled claim), and no timeout-based activation (the timeout-activation claim) involved.
